name: Discovery
desc: the actor maps the cloud account by listing or describing identities, roles, permission policies, compute instances, storage, networks and security settings. The calls are almost all read-only and are spread across many resource types or services in a short time. Unlike routine monitoring, it sweeps broadly to learn what exists instead of repeatedly checking a few known resources.
api_examples: ListUsers, ListRoles, GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, DescribeInstances, DescribeSnapshots, ListBuckets

Unlike routine monitoring, it sweeps broadly to learn what exists instead of repeatedly checking a few known resources.

name: Persistence and Privilege Escalation
desc: the actor changes identities so it can keep access or gain more power. For persistence, it issues new access keys or console passwords, or creates users and groups, so it can come back later. For privilege escalation, it attaches, replaces, edits or deletes permission policies or group memberships to gain broader rights. These are write operations on identity and access settings, often several in a row on the same user, group or policy, and unlike planned administration they widen or secure the actor's own access.
api_examples: CreateAccessKey, CreateLoginProfile, UpdateLoginProfile, CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, PutRolePolicy, CreatePolicyVersion, SetDefaultPolicyVersion, DeletePolicy, DeleteGroup

name: Initial Access and Stealth
desc: the actor gets in and then hides behind a legitimate identity. For initial access, it signs in through a federated single sign-on login or takes on a role it was not expected to use. For stealth, it then keeps working under that trusted-looking identity so its calls blend in with those of normal users. The warning sign is who is acting and how they got in, not an unusual operation.

name: Credential Access
desc: the actor tries to obtain secrets it can reuse, such as stored passwords, secret values, encrypted parameters, access keys or instance passwords. The log shows reads from secret or key stores or attempts to retrieve credentials, sometimes many in a row or with access-denied failures. Unlike an application reading its own configuration, the requests reach for many credentials the identity does not normally use.
api_examples: GetSecretValue, BatchGetSecretValue, GetParameters with decryption, GetPasswordData

name: Benign
desc: routine work by authorized people, pipelines or service roles, such as scheduled monitoring that checks the same resources again and again, automated jobs and service roles doing their configured tasks, software deployments and planned maintenance. The calls follow a steady, repetitive pattern under expected identities and do not widen access, hide activity, or touch secrets or stored data unusually.

name: Defense Impairment
desc: the actor weakens the account's defenses so that later actions go unnoticed or unblocked, for example by stopping, deleting or narrowing audit and network logging, disabling threat detection, or opening firewall rules and network access lists to the whole internet. The log shows changes to logging, security services or network rules rather than to business resources. Legitimate changes to these settings are rare and planned.
api_examples: StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, PutEventSelectors, DeleteDetector, AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, CreateNetworkAclEntry

name: Impact
desc: the actor damages the owner's data or resources or abuses them at the owner's expense, for example by encrypting stored data with a key the owner does not control, deleting data, backups or instances, or running costly services at large scale. The log shows destructive or encrypting write operations on storage and resources, often repeated across many objects. Unlike normal cleanup, it targets data and resources the owner still needs.
api_examples: PutObject with a customer-provided key, DeleteObjects, DeleteBucket, DeleteSnapshot, InvokeModel

name: Collection
desc: the actor gathers data from cloud storage before taking it out, reading or downloading many stored objects or files, often from buckets the identity does not normally use. The log shows bursts of read access to stored data rather than to configuration. Unlike an application reading its own files, the reads are broad and come from an unexpected identity.

name: Exfiltration
desc: the actor moves data out of the owner's control, for example by sharing snapshots, machine images or databases with an outside account, or by changing bucket policies so others can read the data. The log shows permission or sharing changes on data-holding resources that point to an unfamiliar account or the public. Unlike normal sharing, the target account is not part of the organization.

name: Execution
desc: the actor runs its own commands or code inside the cloud account, for example by sending shell commands to instances through a management service or by creating or updating serverless functions with new code. The log shows command or code deployment requests followed by checks on their results. Unlike planned deployments, the code or commands come from an unexpected identity and are not part of a release.

name: Lateral Movement
desc: the actor moves from the cloud control plane into running machines, for example by pushing temporary login keys to an instance or opening a remote shell or serial console session. The log shows remote-access requests aimed at specific instances. Unlike routine administration, the access comes from an identity that does not normally log into those machines.
